topics.name: Classification and Structure of Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
topics.summary: Haloalkanes and haloarenes are classified in two ways. By the number of halogen atoms, a compound is mono-, di-, or polyhalogenated. By the hybridisation of the halogen-bearing carbon, monohalogen compounds split into two families: those with an sp3 C–X bond (alkyl halides, R–X), and those with an sp2 C–X bond (vinylic halides, where X sits directly on a C=C carbon, and aryl halides, where X sits directly on the aromatic ring). Alkyl halides are further split by how many carbons are attached to the halogen-bearing carbon: primary (1°), secondary (2°), or tertiary (3°). Two special sp3 cases deserve care: allylic halides have X on the saturated carbon adjacent to a C=C double bond, and benzylic halides have X on the saturated carbon attached to an aromatic ring. Getting these six labels right is the foundation for predicting reactivity later in the chapter.
topics.worked_example:
Classify CH2=CH–CH2–Cl.
Step 1: Locate the halogen – it is on a CH2 carbon.
Step 2: Is that carbon part of the C=C bond itself? No – the double bond is between the first two carbons; Cl is on the third, saturated carbon.
Step 3: Since the Cl-bearing carbon is sp3 and directly adjacent to the double bond, this is an allylic halide (allyl chloride), not vinylic.
common_mistakes: Assuming any halogen near a double bond or ring is automatically 'allylic', without checking whether X sits ON the sp<sup>2</sup> carbon (vinylic/aryl) or on the adjacent sp<sup>3</sup> carbon (allylic/benzylic).

Confusing benzylic halides (X on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon attached to a ring, e.g. C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl) with aryl halides (X directly on the ring, e.g. C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl).
Miscounting the carbon substituents on the halogen-bearing carbon when assigning primary/secondary/tertiary, especially in branched structures.

topics.name: IUPAC Nomenclature of Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
topics.summary: IUPAC substitutive nomenclature names haloalkanes as halo-substituted hydrocarbons: identify the longest chain containing the halogen-bearing carbon, number it to give the lowest locant set, and cite the halogen as a prefix (fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-) in alphabetical order among substituents. When two numbering directions give the same locant set, the substituent cited first alphabetically gets the lower number. For monohalobenzenes, the common and IUPAC names coincide (e.g. bromobenzene); for dihalobenzenes, IUPAC uses numeral locants (1,2-; 1,3-; 1,4-) in place of the common o-/m-/p- prefixes. Dihaloalkanes with both halogens on the same carbon are geminal (gem-) dihalides (IUPAC: 1,1-dihalo...); with halogens on adjacent carbons they are vicinal (vic-) dihalides (IUPAC: 1,2-dihalo...). Careful chain selection and lowest-locant reasoning – not just pattern-matching to a similar-looking name – is essential for branched and polyfunctional substrates.
key_formulas: Lowest-locant rule: choose the numbering direction giving the lower locant set at first point of difference
Tie-break: lower locant to the substituent cited first alphabetically
topics.worked_example:
Name (CH3)3C–CH2–Cl.
Step 1: Longest chain through the quaternary carbon = 3 carbons (propane), not 4, since the quaternary carbon has no continuous 4-carbon path other than via a methyl branch.
Step 2: Number from the Cl end: C1 (CH2Cl) – C2 (C, bearing two CH3 branches) – C3 (CH3).
Step 3: Name = 1-chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane.
common_mistakes: Extending the parent chain incorrectly through a branch instead of finding the true longest continuous chain (e.g. calling neopentyl chloride a 'butane' derivative).
Failing to apply the lowest-locant-set rule, numbering from the wrong end so a substituent gets a higher locant than necessary.
Confusing gem- and vic-dihalide classification and their corresponding 1,1- vs 1,2- locants.

topics.name: Nature of the C–X Bond and Physical Properties
topics.summary: The C–X bond is polarised (Cδ+–Xδ−) because halogens are more electronegative than carbon. Down the halogen group, atomic size increases (F<Cl<Br<I), so C–X bond length and dipole moment trends follow accordingly, while bond enthalpy decreases. Physically, methyl/ethyl chlorides and bromides are gases, but higher members are liquids/solids; for a given alkyl group, boiling point rises R–F<R–Cl<R–Br<R–I because van der Waals forces strengthen with halogen size and polarizability. Among isomers, more branching lowers boiling point (less surface area for van der Waals contact). Haloalkanes are only slightly water-soluble (breaking water's hydrogen bonds costs more energy than is regained) but dissolve well in organic solvents. Density rises with halogen mass and count; bromo/iodo/polychloro derivatives are typically denser than water. Symmetric para-dihalobenzenes have distinctly higher melting points than ortho/meta isomers due to more efficient crystal packing, not bond-strength or dipole differences.
key_formulas: Boiling point (same R): R–F < R–Cl < R–Br < R–I
Bond length: C–F(139 pm) < C–Cl(178) < C–Br(193) < C–I(214)
topics.worked_example:
Rank the boiling points of the three isomeric bromobutanes: 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
Step 1: Recognise all three share the same formula (C4H9Br), so mass/polarity alone won't distinguish them.
Step 2: More branching → less molecular surface area → weaker van der Waals contact → lower boiling point.
Step 3: Order: 1-bromobutane (375 K, straight-chain) > 2-bromobutane > 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (346 K, most branched).
common_mistakes: Reversing the halogen-size/boiling-point trend, e.g. believing R–F boils highest since fluorine is 'most reactive'.
Assuming branching increases boiling point, rather than recognising it lowers boiling point by reducing van der Waals contact area.
Attributing the high melting point of para-dihalobenzenes to a larger dipole moment, when in fact its dipole is smaller (more symmetric) and the real cause is crystal-packing efficiency.

topics.name: Methods of Preparation of Haloalkanes
topics.summary: Alkyl halides are prepared from (i) alcohols, by substituting –OH with halogen acids (HCl needs ZnCl2 for 1°/2° alcohols but not 3°), phosphorus halides (PX3, PCl5, or red P + X2 generated in situ), or SOCl2 (preferred, since both by-products SO2 and HCl escape as gases, giving pure product); (ii) hydrocarbons, via free-radical halogenation of alkanes (Cl2/UV, giving a mixture of isomers, so poor for a single pure product), or addition of HX or X2 to alkenes (Markovnikov's rule governs HX addition regiochemistry); and (iii) halogen exchange – the Finkelstein reaction (NaI in dry acetone, converting R–Cl/Br to R–I as NaCl/NaBr precipitates, driving the equilibrium forward) and the Swarts reaction (AgF/Hg2F2/CoF2/SbF3, converting R–Cl/Br to R–F). Reactivity of alcohols toward a given haloacid follows 3°>2°>1°, mirroring carbocation stability. These methods do NOT work for phenols, since the aryl C–O bond resists cleavage.
topics.worked_example:
Why is SOCl2 preferred over HCl/ZnCl2 for converting a primary alcohol to its chloride?
Step 1: Both give R–Cl, but HCl/ZnCl2 leaves ZnCl2/water residues that must be separated from the product.
Step 2: SOCl2 gives R–Cl + SO2↑ + HCl↑ – both by-products are gases that simply escape.
Step 3: The alkyl chloride is therefore obtained in a purer state with SOCl2.
common_mistakes: Assuming conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is a harmless proton source in R–OH + NaI/H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> preparations, when in fact H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> would oxidise the iodide product to I<sub>2</sub>, consuming the nucleophile.
Mixing up the Finkelstein (NaI, dry acetone → alkyl iodide) and Swarts (AgF/SbF<sub>3</sub> → alkyl fluoride) halogen-exchange reactions.
Expecting free-radical chlorination of an alkane to give one clean product, rather than recognising it gives a mixture whenever more than one distinct hydrogen environment exists.

topics.name: Methods of Preparation of Haloarenes
topics.summary: Aryl halides cannot be made by the alcohol-substitution routes used for alkyl halides, because phenol's C–O bond has partial double-bond character (from ring resonance) and resists cleavage. Instead, two main routes are used. (i) Electrophilic substitution of an arene with X2 in the presence of a Lewis acid (Fe or FeCl3) gives ortho/para products (separable by their differing melting points); fluoro compounds are not made this way since F2 is too vigorous. (ii) Diazonium chemistry: a primary aromatic amine is diazotised (NaNO2/HX, 273–278 K) to a diazonium salt, which is then treated with Cu2Cl2/Cu2Br2 (Sandmeyer reaction) for Cl/Br, or simply shaken with KI (no catalyst needed) for iodide. These routes matter because they are the only practical ways to introduce halogen directly onto an otherwise unfunctionalised or amine-bearing aromatic ring.
key_formulas: ArH + X<sub>2</sub> —Fe/dark→ Ar–X + HX (X = Cl, Br)
topics.worked_example:
How is iodobenzene best prepared from aniline?
Step 1: Diazotise aniline with NaNO2/HCl at 273–278 K to form benzenediazonium chloride.
Step 2: Shake the diazonium salt with KI – no cuprous catalyst is needed for iodide (unlike Cl/Br).
Step 3: N2 gas is released and iodobenzene is obtained.
common_mistakes: Trying to prepare an aryl halide by treating phenol directly with HX, not recognising that the resonance-strengthened aryl C–O bond blocks this route.
Assuming the Sandmeyer reaction's cuprous-halide catalyst is also required for the KI/diazonium route to aryl iodides, when it is not.
Believing ortho/para-halotoluene isomers from electrophilic bromination cannot be separated, when their melting-point difference makes separation practical.

topics.name: Nucleophilic Substitution: SN2 Mechanism and Kinetics
topics.summary: The SN2 (substitution nucleophilic bimolecular) mechanism is a single, concerted step: the nucleophile attacks the substrate carbon from the side directly opposite the leaving group (backside attack), while the C–X bond breaks simultaneously with C–Nu bond formation. No intermediate forms; the rate law is second order overall (first order in substrate, first order in nucleophile). Because the transition state is crowded (five groups partially bonded to carbon), steric hindrance dominates reactivity: CH3X > 1° > 2° > 3° (roughly 30:1:0.02:~0 for methyl:ethyl:isopropyl:tert-butyl). At a stereocentre, SN2 gives clean inversion of configuration (Walden inversion) – but note that inversion of configuration does not automatically mean the sign of optical rotation flips, since rotation sign and spatial configuration are not simply linked. Even branching one carbon away from the reacting centre (as in neopentyl halides) can slow SN2 dramatically through steric hindrance to the approaching nucleophile.
topics.worked_example:
Predict the stereochemical outcome when (R)-2-bromobutane reacts with NaOH via SN2.
Step 1: SN2 proceeds by backside attack, opposite the leaving Br.
Step 2: This inverts the spatial arrangement at the reacting carbon.
Step 3: The product is (S)-butan-2-ol, a single, stereospecific product – not a racemic mixture.
common_mistakes: Believing SN2 rate increases with branching/steric bulk, rather than recognising that increased steric hindrance around the reacting carbon slows backside attack.
Confusing SN2's inversion outcome with SN1's racemisation outcome, or assuming inversion of configuration must flip the sign of optical rotation.
Overlooking those braches one carbon removed from the reacting centre (e.g. neopentyl-type substrates) that still sterically block SN2 even though the halogen-bearing carbon itself is primary.

topics.name: Nucleophilic Substitution: SN1 Mechanism, Carbocation Stability, and Stereochemistry
topics.summary: The SN1 (substitution nucleophilic unimolecular) mechanism proceeds in two steps: a slow, rate-determining ionisation of R–X to a planar, sp2 carbocation plus X−, followed by fast nucleophilic attack on the carbocation. The rate law is first order, depending only on substrate concentration (not on the nucleophile), and the reaction is favoured by polar protic solvents that stabilise the ionic intermediates. Reactivity tracks carbocation stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH3X, with allylic/benzylic halides reacting unusually fast due to resonance stabilisation of the cation. Because the planar carbocation can be attacked from either face, SN1 at a stereocentre gives racemisation – a near 50:50 mixture of both configurations – in sharp contrast to SN2's clean inversion. Vinylic and aryl halides cannot undergo SN1 (or SN2) because the corresponding vinyl/phenyl cation cannot be resonance-stabilised and is far too unstable to form.
key_formulas: Rate = k[substrate] (first order, independent of nucleophile)
Carbocation stability/SN1 rate: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH<sub>3</sub>X; allylic/benzylic enhanced by resonance
topics.worked_example:
Predict the stereochemical outcome when optically active 2-bromobutane undergoes SN1 hydrolysis.
Step 1: Slow ionisation gives a planar, achiral carbocation.
Step 2: Water can attack from either face of the planar cation with roughly equal probability.
Step 3: The product is (±)-butan-2-ol – a racemic mixture, not a single stereospecific product.
common_mistakes: Assigning inversion of configuration (SN2's signature) to an SN1 reaction, instead of the correct racemisation outcome from the planar carbocation.
Believing SN1 rate depends on nucleophile concentration/strength, when the rate-determining step (ionisation) involves only the substrate.

Confusing the highly stabilised benzylic/allylic cation (charge delocalised into an exocyclic conjugated system) with the highly unstable phenyl/vinyl cation (charge in-plane, not conjugated with the ring π system).

topics.name: Factors Affecting Nucleophilic Substitution Reactivity
topics.summary: Whether a substrate follows SN1 or SN2 depends jointly on: (i) substrate structure – steric bulk disfavours SN2, while carbocation-stabilising substitution/resonance favours SN1; (ii) nucleophile – strong, small, high-concentration nucleophiles favour SN2 (whose rate law includes nucleophile concentration), while weak nucleophiles favour SN1 (whose rate does not depend on nucleophile at all); (iii) solvent – polar protic solvents stabilise SN1's ionic intermediates; and (iv) leaving-group ability (I−>Br−>Cl−>>F−), which speeds both mechanisms, just at different steps. Secondary substrates are genuinely borderline, reacting by either pathway depending on conditions. Ambident nucleophiles (CN−, NO2−) can attack through either atom: the more ionic KCN gives the nitrile (C-attack, more stable C–C bond) while the more covalent AgCN gives the isocyanide (N-attack).
key_formulas: SN2 favoured by: strong/small Nu, high [Nu], polar aprotic solvent, low steric bulk
SN1 favoured by: weak Nu, polar protic solvent, stable carbocation (3°/allylic/benzylic)
topics.worked_example:
Predict the major pathway: a secondary alkyl bromide reacts with a weak nucleophile in aqueous ethanol, no added base.
Step 1: Weak nucleophile → rules out a fast, concentration-dependent SN2 pathway.
Step 2: Polar protic solvent (aqueous ethanol) stabilises ionic intermediates.
Step 3: These conditions together point to SN1 as the dominant pathway.
common_mistakes: Applying carbocation-stability reasoning to predict SN2 rates, when SN2 rate is governed by steric hindrance, not carbocation stability.
Assuming nucleophile concentration affects SN1 rate, when the SN1 rate-determining step (ionisation) does not involve the nucleophile at all.
Assuming KCN and AgCN give the same major product, rather than recognising that ionic/covalent character of the reagent determines C- versus N-attack.

topics.name: Elimination Reactions and Reactions with Metals
topics.summary: Haloalkanes with a β-hydrogen undergo β-elimination with alcoholic KOH: a β-hydrogen and the α-halogen are removed to form an alkene. When more than one β-hydrogen type is available, Zaitsev's (Saytzeff's) rule predicts the major product as the more substituted (more stable) alkene, though bulky bases can shift the ratio toward the less-substituted alkene by preferentially abstracting the more sterically accessible β-hydrogen. Substitution and elimination are competing pathways for the same alkyl halide + base/nucleophile; the outcome depends on substrate branching, and the base/nucleophile's strength, size, and the solvent. Separately, alkyl halides react with reactive metals: Mg in dry ether gives Grignard reagents (RMgX, polar covalent C–Mg, ionic Mg–X), which react violently with any proton source (water, alcohols, amines) to give RH; Na in dry ether gives the Wurtz reaction (2RX → R–R, symmetrical alkanes only from a single halide).
key_formulas: β-elimination: R–CH<sub>2</sub>–CHX–R' + alc. KOH → R–CH=CH–R' + KX + H<sub>2</sub>O
topics.worked_example:
Predict the major product when 2-bromopentane reacts with alcoholic KOH.
Step 1: Identify available β-hydrogens – on C1 (giving pent-1-ene) and on C3 (giving pent-2-ene).
Step 2: Pent-2-ene is disubstituted at the double bond; pent-1-ene is monosubstituted.
Step 3: By Zaitsev's rule, pent-2-ene (more substituted) is the major product (81%), with pent-1-ene as minor (19%).
common_mistakes: Applying Markovnikov's rule (an addition-reaction concept) to predict elimination selectivity, instead of Zaitsev's rule.
Assuming Grignard reagents are unreactive/stable toward moisture, rather than recognising their extreme reactivity toward any proton source, which is exactly why anhydrous conditions are essential.
Expecting a Wurtz reaction on a mixture of two different alkyl halides to give one clean product, rather than a mixture including the unsymmetrical cross-product.

topics.name: Reactivity and Reactions of Haloarenes
topics.summary: Haloarenes are far less reactive than haloalkanes toward nucleophilic substitution, for three linked reasons: (i) resonance donation of a halogen lone pair into the ring gives the C–X bond partial double-bond character (shorter, stronger: 169 pm vs 177 pm for an alkyl C–Cl); (ii) the sp2 carbon holds electrons more tightly than an sp3 carbon; and (iii) the phenyl cation that would form on ionisation is not resonance-stabilised, ruling out SN1. Unactivated chlorobenzene needs extreme conditions (623 K, 300 atm NaOH) to give phenol, but an electron-withdrawing group (–NO2) at ortho/para (not meta) dramatically activates the ring by stabilising the anionic intermediate through resonance. For electrophilic substitution, halogens are unusual: net ring-deactivating (inductive withdrawal dominates the overall rate) yet ortho/para-directing (resonance donation controls where attack occurs).
key_formulas: Aryl C–Cl (169 pm) < alkyl C–Cl (177 pm)
−NO<sub>2</sub> at o-/p- activates toward nucleophilic substitution; at m-, little/no effect
topics.worked_example:
Explain why p-nitrochlorobenzene hydrolyses to p-nitrophenol far more easily than chlorobenzene hydrolyses to phenol.
Step 1: Nucleophilic attack by OH− forms a carbanion intermediate.
Step 2: With –NO2 at the para position, a resonance structure places the negative charge directly on the nitro group's oxygen, stabilising the intermediate.
Step 3: This lowers the activation energy substantially, allowing much milder reaction conditions than for unactivated chlorobenzene.
common_mistakes: Believing haloarenes are more, or equally, reactive toward nucleophilic substitution as haloalkanes, rather than markedly less reactive.
Labelling halogens as meta-directors because they are net deactivating, instead of recognising their ortho/para-directing resonance effect operates independently of their net inductive deactivation.

Expecting a meta-positioned –NO<sub>2</sub> group to activate a haloarene the same way an ortho/para-positioned one does, missing that only ortho/para resonance structures place charge on the nitro-bearing carbon.

topics.name: Polyhalogen Compounds and Environmental Impact
topics.summary: Polyhalogen compounds have varied industrial uses but several raise environmental/health concerns rooted in their chemical stability. Dichloromethane is a paint-remover/aerosol solvent that harms the nervous system on exposure. Chloroform is used as a solvent and freon-22 precursor; it slowly oxidises in air/light to poisonous phosgene (COCl2), so it is stored in dark, filled bottles. Iodoform's antiseptic action comes from liberated free iodine, not the molecule itself. Carbon tetrachloride, once a common cleaning fluid, is linked to liver toxicity and, on reaching the stratosphere, contributes to ozone depletion. Freons (stable, unreactive, non-toxic, easily liquefiable chlorofluorocarbons, e.g. Freon-12 from CCl4 via the Swarts reaction) were valued for refrigeration/propellants but also deplete stratospheric ozone. DDT's chemical stability and fat solubility, which made it an effective long-lasting insecticide, are exactly what cause it to bioaccumulate in fatty tissue and persist in the environment.
topics.worked_example:
Explain why chloroform is stored in dark, completely filled bottles.
Step 1: In the presence of light and air, chloroform is slowly oxidised.
Step 2: The oxidation product is phosgene (carbonyl chloride, COCl2), an extremely poisonous gas.
Step 3: Excluding light and air (dark, filled bottles) prevents this decomposition, keeping the stored chloroform safe.
common_mistakes: Assuming carbon tetrachloride is non-toxic, when it is in fact linked to nervous-system and liver effects, and ozone depletion.
Believing DDT's environmental persistence and its insecticidal effectiveness are unrelated properties, rather than two consequences of the same underlying chemical stability.
Confusing which specific decomposition pathway (chloroform's light/air oxidation to phosgene) applies to which polyhalogen compound.

questions.topic: Classification and Structure of Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
questions.question: In an alkyl halide R–X, the halogen is bonded to which type of carbon?
options: A carbon bonded to oxygen
An sp hybridised carbon
An sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised carbon
An sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon
questions.explanation: Alkyl halides (haloalkanes) are defined by a halogen attached to an sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised carbon; haloarenes and vinylic halides instead involve sp<sup>2</sup> carbons.
questions.hint: Think about the hybridisation that defines a haloALKANE.
distractor_logic: Confuses halogen substitution with oxygen-containing functional groups such as alcohols.
sp carbons are not part of this basic mono-halogen classification scheme.
Confuses haloalkanes (sp<sup>3</sup> C–X) with haloarenes/vinylic halides, which have sp<sup>2</sup> C–X.

questions.topic: Classification and Structure of Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
questions.question: CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–Br is best classified as a:
options: Vinylic halide
Secondary (2°) monohaloalkane
Primary (1°) monohaloalkane
Tertiary (3°) monohaloalkane
questions.explanation: The Br-bearing carbon is attached to only one other carbon, making this a primary monohaloalkane.
questions.hint: Count how many other carbons are attached to the C–Br carbon.
distractor_logic: Wrongly applies the vinylic label, which requires X on an sp<sup>2</sup> alkene carbon, to a saturated chain.
Mistakes the terminal –CH<sub>2</sub>Br carbon (attached to only one other carbon) for a secondary carbon.
Wrongly assumes any chain longer than 2 carbons must be tertiary, ignoring the actual substitution at the C–Br carbon.

questions.topic: Classification and Structure of Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
questions.question: Which structure represents an allylic halide?
options: CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–Br
CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>–Br
C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–Br
C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–Br
questions.explanation: An allylic halide has X on the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon directly adjacent to a C=C double bond, as in CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>Br.
questions.hint: Look for X on the saturated carbon next to a double bond, not on the double bond itself.
distractor_logic: This is a vinylic halide (X on the sp<sup>2</sup> alkene carbon itself), not allylic.
This is an aryl halide, with X directly on the aromatic ring.
This is a benzylic halide (X on the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon attached to the ring), often confused with allylic.

questions.topic: IUPAC Nomenclature of Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
questions.question: The IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br is:
options: Propyl chloride
1-Bromopropane
n-Propyl bromide
2-Bromopropane
questions.explanation: Numbering from the end nearest the substituent gives Br the lowest locant, C1.
questions.hint: Number the chain from the end that gives Br the lowest locant.
distractor_logic: Confuses the halogen itself (chloride instead of bromide).
Gives the common name instead of the IUPAC substitutive name.
Misplaces the locant, numbering from the wrong end so Br appears on C2 instead of the terminal C1.

questions.question: IUPAC name of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr?
options: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane
2-Methyl-2-bromobutane
1-Bromo-2-methylpropane
tert-Butyl bromide

questions.hint: Identify the longest chain first, then locate Br on the central carbon.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly extends the parent chain to four carbons (butane) instead of the correct three-carbon propane.
Misassigns the locant of Br, placing it on C1 instead of the central, most substituted C2.
Correct compound, but this is the common name, not the IUPAC name requested.

options: Chloroethene
1-Chloroethane
Vinyl chloride
Chloroethyne

questions.hint: Check whether the parent hydrocarbon has a double bond, single bond, or triple bond.
distractor_logic: Wrongly names the compound as a saturated haloalkane (ethane), ignoring the C=C double bond.
This is the common name, not the IUPAC name.
Wrongly assigns a triple bond (-yne) when the molecule contains a double bond (-ene).

questions.topic: IUPAC Nomenclature of Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
questions.question: For dihalogen-substituted benzene, IUPAC nomenclature indicates ring positions using:
options: Roman numerals I, II, III
Greek letters α, β
Numerals such as 1,2-; 1,3-; 1,4-
The prefixes ortho-, meta-, para- only
questions.explanation: IUPAC substitutive nomenclature uses locant numerals (1,2-; 1,3-; 1,4-) rather than the common o-/m-/p- prefixes.
questions.hint: o-/m-/p- are common-name shorthand, not IUPAC locants.
distractor_logic: Roman numerals are not part of standard IUPAC locant notation.
Greek-letter locants are used informally for chain positions relative to a functional group, not ring substitution.
o-/m-/p- prefixes are the common-name convention; IUPAC instead uses locant numerals.

questions.topic: Nature of the C–X Bond and Physical Properties
questions.question: The C–X bond in alkyl halides is polarised such that:
options: Carbon bears a partial positive charge (δ+) and halogen a partial negative charge (δ−)
The bond is completely non-polar
Carbon bears δ− and halogen bears δ+
Both atoms are equally and oppositely charged as full ions
questions.explanation: Halogen, being more electronegative than carbon, pulls electron density toward itself, leaving carbon δ+ and halogen δ−.
questions.hint: Which atom is more electronegative, carbon or the halogen?
distractor_logic: Ignores the substantial electronegativity difference between carbon and halogen.
Reverses the polarity — the more electronegative halogen pulls electron density toward itself, not away.
The C–X bond is a polar covalent bond with partial charges, not a fully ionic bond.

questions.topic: Nature of the C–X Bond and Physical Properties
questions.question: Among CH<sub>3</sub>F, CH<sub>3</sub>Cl, CH<sub>3</sub>Br, and CH<sub>3</sub>I, which has the shortest C–X bond length?
options: CH<sub>3</sub>F
CH<sub>3</sub>Br
CH<sub>3</sub>Cl
CH<sub>3</sub>I
questions.explanation: Bond length increases with halogen atomic size (F<Cl<Br<I), so CH<sub>3</sub>F has the shortest C–X bond.
questions.hint: Bond length tracks the size of the halogen atom.
distractor_logic: Bromine's still larger radius gives an even longer C–Br bond.
Chlorine's larger atomic radius than fluorine gives a longer bond, not the shortest.
Iodine, the largest halogen here, gives the longest C–X bond, the opposite of shortest.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Haloalkanes
questions.question: Which reagent, reacted with an alcohol, is preferred for preparing pure alkyl chlorides because both by-products escape as gases?
options: PCl<sub>3</sub>
NaCl
SOCl<sub>2</sub> (thionyl chloride)
Conc. HCl alone (no catalyst)
